tagline.text: A neoclassical church in the heart of Dasmariñas that still carries the memory of the 1897 battle

location.label: Location
location.text: Don Placido Campos Avenue, Poblacion, Dasmariñas City, Cavite

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season, December 8 feast day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (round-trip transport from Manila included, per person)

children.text: Standing in the middle of Dasmariñas Poblacion, this is the first Catholic parish church in the city, built after the parish was created by royal order in 1866. With its four-story bell towers and neoclassical facade, it is a historic site that holds the memory of both the 1897 battle and the 1944 killings.

Immaculate Conception Parish Church sits right in the middle of the Poblacion (old town center) of Dasmariñas City in Cavite Province. Its formal name is the Immaculate Conception Parish Church, and in Filipino it is called Parokya ng La Inmaculada Concepcion. It belongs to the Diocese of Imus and is the first Catholic parish church ever established in the city. It stands close to City Hall and the plaza, so it is an easy stop when you are passing through town.

This area belonged to the Hacienda de Imus run by the Augustinian Recollects during the Spanish colonial period, and it began as a small chapel attached to the Imus parish. Perez-Dasmariñas became a separate town on May 12, 1864, and Queen Isabella II signed the royal order creating the parish on October 21, 1866. The parish was actually established from 1867, with the Recollect priest Valentin Diaz serving as its first parish priest. The town's patroness is Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, and the stone church is said to have been built right after the parish was founded.

The building is neoclassical in style. The facade has a portico over a semicircular arched main door, flanked by four-story bell towers. The lower two stories are square and the upper two are octagonal, and thick buttresses reinforce the side walls so they can withstand earthquakes. The church is about
long and

wide, built of stone, brick and wood. It has been renovated many times over the years, so much of its original appearance has changed; photos from the late Spanish period show a much simpler facade with no bell towers.

This is a place where you read the story, not just look at the building. On February 25, 1897, the Battle of Perez-Dasmariñas was fought here at the church and convent between Philippine revolutionary forces and Spanish troops, and during the Japanese occupation in 1944 the church served as a temporary garrison, where suspected guerrillas were killed. In 1986 the National Historical Institute, the predecessor of the National Historical Commission, installed a historical marker and designated it a protected structure. Rather than expecting a big attraction, think of it as a quiet stop for tracing Cavite's history, and you will likely be satisfied.

blocks.title: Neoclassical facade with four-story bell towers

children.text: A semicircular arched entrance with a portico, flat pilasters, arched windows of different sizes, a triangular pediment and a small round window rise in three stories. The bell towers on both sides are square below and octagonal above, so their outline stands out even from far away. The best spot for photos is on the plaza side, where the whole facade fits into a single frame.

Inside the church is a statue of the Immaculate Conception said to have been carved in 1867 by the sculptor Esperidion Arevalo. The statue is revered as the patroness of the city, and on December 7, 2002, Bishop Emeritus Manuel Sobreviñas held a coronation ceremony for it. Even if you are not a believer, you can quietly view it when Mass is not in progress.

There are two bells: the small one dates from around 1867, and the larger one is known to have been cast in 1890 at the Hilario Sunico Foundry in Manila. The small bell is said to carry an inscription giving its date. The bell towers are not open to the public, so looking up at them from below is enough.

blocks.title: The historical marker and the memory of the 1897 battle

children.text: On February 25, 1897, Spanish troops attacked the revolutionaries who had taken refuge in the church and convent, and the Philippine forces led by Placido Campos and Francisco Barzaga were defeated. The Spanish burned the town except for the church, which was later used as a garrison. You can read a brief account of this story on the historical marker installed in 1986.
Inside are a retablo on the main altar and stained glass, and the mood becomes softer when daylight comes in. The nave is wide at about
, and records mention that a major renovation including raising the ceiling is under way, so please check the condition of the church when you visit.

blocks.title: The town center beside City Hall and the plaza

children.text: The church stands in the Poblacion, where the plaza, City Hall, the library and an elementary school are clustered. Rather than seeing only the church, it works well as a short walking route that includes a loop around the plaza. It is the oldest public space in town, so you can also take in local daily life.

blocks.title: The December 8 Feast of the Immaculate Conception

children.text: Every year on December 8 the Poblacion celebrates the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception on a grand scale, with colorful banners, marching bands and fireworks that lift the whole city. A solemn Mass and procession are followed by community events. If you want to feel the local atmosphere, this is the best day, but it is also the most crowded.
Arrive in the Poblacion and photograph the whole facade from the plaza in front of the church. Look for a spot where you can see the octagonal upper parts of the bell towers and the arched windows.
Find and read the 1986 historical marker near the main entrance. If you know the story of the 1897 battle and the Japanese occupation before you go in, the interior looks different.

If no Mass is in progress, quietly go inside and take your time looking at the nave, the altar, the stained glass and the statue of the Immaculate Conception. Take photos so that people who are praying do not appear in them.
Walk around the back and sides of the church to see the thick buttresses and traces of the convent building. Part of the convent is now parish office space, so do not go in without permission.
Walk around City Hall and the plaza, and take a break with a snack or a drink at a nearby shop.
The surest way to check the Mass schedule is the parish Facebook page or similar. When Mass is in full swing, it may be hard to enter for sightseeing.
Set out from Manila and look around the church in Dasmariñas Poblacion first.
Travel by car to Imus and see the area around Imus Cathedral (Our Lady of the Pillar). Imus is the seat of the diocese that covers all of Cavite.
Have lunch in Imus town.
If you have time left, visit more of Cavite's historic sites, such as the Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit. Travel times vary greatly with traffic, so leave some margin.
Traffic around Cavite is very heavy during rush hours. When combining several places in one day, it is best to keep to two or three a day.

items.title: From Manila by bus and jeepney

children.text: From southern Manila (Pasay, Buendia) take a bus or UV Express bound for Cavite to Dasmariñas. Routes and terminals change often, so check locally.
After getting off in Dasmariñas, switch to a jeepney or tricycle toward the Poblacion (City Hall and church). Aguinaldo Highway (National Highway 17) runs through the city.
From Manila to Dasmariñas it is about
30km
in a straight line, but some sources give the road distance as about
50km
. Allow about
1.5–3 hours
depending on weekday traffic.
Bus and UV fares and routes must be checked locally.
Drive via Aguinaldo Highway or a Cavite-bound expressway to the Poblacion. Enter Immaculate Conception Parish Church Dasmariñas in your navigation app.

The area along Placido Campos Avenue in front of the church can be congested. Parking is along the streets around the church or in spaces near City Hall, and during Mass and on feast days there are almost no spaces.
Ride-hailing services such as Grab can be hard to connect depending on the area and time, so think ahead about your ride back.
Walking and tricycles are enough within the Poblacion. The church, plaza and City Hall are close together.
When coming from other areas, check for jeepneys heading to the Poblacion. Ask the driver to drop you at City Hall or in front of the church.

Dasmariñas has a tropical climate with distinct dry and wet seasons. November to May is relatively dry and good for walking around the church, and January to April is usually the clearest. Daytime highs stay around
all year, so midday is hot.

The special day is the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception on December 8. It is the best day to see the local festival atmosphere, but it is crowded and traffic is heavy, so allow plenty of time for your schedule and transport. For quiet photography and viewing the interior, weekday mornings are better.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: December 8 feast day and Christmas season events. Can be crowded with Masses and events
Midday sun is strong, so a morning visit is recommended. Many events during Holy Week
August has the most rainfall. Bring an umbrella; the city is crowded during the Paru-Paro Festival on November 26

The church itself is a day-trip place that does not require an overnight stay. Most people come from Manila and go back the same day; if you want to stay a night, choose a place in Dasmariñas town or in nearby Imus or Tagaytay. Tagaytay requires travel by vehicle, so consider the traffic.

Around the Poblacion there are local eateries, street snacks and bakeries. Meat dishes and soups are common in Cavite, and near the plaza it is a good place to eat lightly and rest. Businesses change often, so pick one on the spot.
During Mass keep quiet so as not to disturb the worshippers, and refrain from using flash or a tripod.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best. Avoid sleeveless tops and short pants.
You can check the Mass schedule through the parish Facebook page or by phone (
), but the number may change.
In the morning the sun lights the facade well and photos turn out nicely. At midday the shadows are strong and facade photos are hard.
If you read the historical marker before going in, you will understand the 1897 battle and the events of 1944 and appreciate the place more.
If you are making a day trip from Manila, leave early in the morning to avoid rush hours and allow for traffic delays on the way back.
On the December 8 feast day and during Holy Week the roads are jammed, so go early or choose another day.
Renovation work inside the church may be under way. Follow the instructions when some areas are restricted.
This church is a place of worship. Sightseeing entry may be restricted during Mass and services, and records mention a major renovation under way, so check the latest announcements before you visit.
Mass schedules and opening hours vary by parish, and we could not confirm specific times from official sources. Check locally.
Roads toward Cavite are very congested during rush hours. Leave plenty of margin in your travel time.
On feast days and during Holy Week, watch out for pickpockets and phone theft, and carry your bag in front of you.
When taking photos around the church, do not secretly photograph local people, and ask permission when possible.
Grab and taxis are hard to get at some times, so decide on your ride back in advance.
It is about
20–40 minutes
away by car. It is the center of the Diocese of Imus, which covers all of Cavite, and you can see the cathedral and the old town together.

The former home of Emilio Aguinaldo in Kawit, it was the stage for the Philippine declaration of independence in 1898. It suits anyone who wants to see Cavite's historic sites together. Travel time varies with traffic.
It is a highland resort famous for views of Taal Lake, and the lake is about
29km
away according to the sources. When combining it in one day, leave early.
A public park along the Imus River in the Burol area. It is described as a good place for a light walk after seeing the church.
